newsitem.title: USA: INTERVIEW - PS Enterprise CFO sees EPS rise.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - PS Enterprise CFO sees EPS rise.

text.p: Public Service Enterprise Group Inc expects earnings per share to increase at least five percent per year over the next five years, Chief Financial Officer Robert C. Murray told Reuters.
But the profit growth will not be translated into increased dividends in the immediate future, he said.
Capital spending by the company's major subsidiary, Public Service Electric & Gas Co, during the next five years "will be half of what was spent in the previous five years," he said in an interview.
Some of that decline will be offset by increased spending by the company's non-regulated activities, he said.
Murray said spending by the utility, excluding nuclear fuel, is expected to drop to $495 million this year, from $592 million in 1996. By 2001, these outlays will be "under $400 million."

But he expects spending by Enterprise's non-regulated generating unit to total $100 to $150 million over the five years, while another $50 to $100 million will be invested by the company's other non-regulated energy businesses.
Last year, about $8 million was spent in these two areas.

Spending on nuclear fuel, which "technically is capital spending," dropped to $45 million from the normal range of $90 to $100 million, Murray said. He noted this reflected the closing of the 42.59 percent-owned Salem Generating Station for the entire year.
PSE&G, the operator of the two 1,106 megawatt units, continues to expect Unit 2 to restart in the second quarter and Unit 1 this summer.

Utility spokesman George Koodray declined to comment on whether PECO Energy Co's stated "belief that the earliest that Unit No. 1 will return to service is late in the third quarter" represents an extention of that timeframe.
The other Salem owners are Atlantic Energy Inc and Delmarva Power and Light Co with 7.41 percent each.
Murray said these plants will be "very competitive" on a cash basis, able to produce power at $0.015-$0.020 per kilowatt hour "on a marginal cost basis."
That is "a lower marginal cost than anything out there."

The plants are a component of Enterprise's earnings growth targets, Murray said, adding the company is "looking for a minimum five percent annual growth (in earnings per share) over the next five years."

Stressing "this is more than a goal," Murray said he's "convinced there's a robustness to (the company's) plans" that will achieve this growth, starting from last year's $2.64 per share, excluding extraordinary items.
The financial community, however, expects Enterprise earnings per share to grow one or two percent per year, he said.
The consensus of the 18 analysts reporting to First Call is $2.69 per share for 1997.

In the short term, Murray said, "The bulk of the (earnings) growth will come from the utility," through further cost reductions. "Beyond the turn of the century," Enterprise's non-regulated power generation and energy services operations will add to the growth, he said.
The chief executive of the newest of those, Energis Resources Inc's Frank Cassiday said he is not expected to produce significant profits for two or three years.
Boosting this year's earnings per share growth will be the repurchase of 13 million shares during the last four months of 1996, Murray said.
The "bulk of (the impact on average shares outstanding) will be this year," he said.

Murray said he does not expect further stock buybacks until the company proceeds with securitization of its stranded assets. This portion of the Energy Master Plan proposed by New Jersey regulators needs legislative approval.

Such sales would probably lead to "massive" repurchases of debt and equity, he said. Since the sales would shrink the company's assets, there would have to be a corresponding shrinkage in its capital, he explained.
Murray also said there will be "no dividend increase in the immediate future."
Although unchanged since 1991, Enterprise's current quarterly payment of $0.54 per share represents a payout ratio of more than 80 percent.
This has to be reduced to between 60 and 70 percent, Murrary said, adding the exact target will depend on Wall Street expectations, once restructuring has been completed.
((-- New York Newsdesk 212-859-1610.))
